parts.title: Ancient Rome
parts.article:
(A) From ancient times to the present, historians have asked the question: How and why did an ordinary little town in central Italy grow so much bigger than any other in the ancient Mediterranean and come to control such a huge empire? During the first century BCE, Roman writers themselves began systematically to study the earlier centuries of their city and their empire. Yet these historians had little more direct evidence of the earliest phases of Rome's history than modern writers have, and in some ways perhaps not as much, as there were no surviving documents or archives. Their 'histories' about the foundation of ancient Rome tell us a good deal about how the Romans saw their city, their values, and their failings. However, they tell us very little indeed about what they claim to inform us about: that is, what earliest Rome was actually like. One fact is obvious. Rome was already a very old city by 63 BCE, the birth date of its first emperor. But how exactly are we to access reliable information about the origins of Rome?

(B) One way of doing this is by turning away from the histories of Roman writers and seeking out clues in the Latin language, or in later Roman institutions that might point back to features of earliest Rome. Much more tangible, however, is the evidence of archaeology. Dig down deep in the city of Rome, below the visible ancient monuments, and a few traces of a much earlier settlement or settlements remain. Beneath the Forum itself (an ancient marketplace at the centre of the city) lie the remains of an early cemetery, which caused tremendous excitement when they were first unearthed at the start of the 20th century. Cemeteries imply the existence of a community, and traces of that are presumably to be found in the groups of huts whose faint outlines have been detected under various parts of the later city, including on the Palatine (the centremost of the seven hills on which Rome is built). We have little idea of the nature of these huts beyond their construction in wood, clay, and thatch, and still less of the lifestyle they supported. But we can fill in some of the gaps if we look just outside Rome. One of the best preserved and most carefully excavated of these early structures was found at Fidenae, a few miles north of the city, in the 1980s. It is a rectangular building, some six by five metres, made of wood and rammed earth - a construction method still utilised up to the present day - with a simple porch around it, formed by the overhanging roof. Inside was a central hearth, some large pottery storage jars, and traces of predictable foodstuffs and domestic animals.

(C) There are vivid glimpses of human and other life here; the question is, what do those glimpses add up to? The archaeological remains certainly demonstrate that there is a long and rich prehistory behind the ancient Rome we can still see, but quite how long that prehistory is is another matter.

(D) Part of the problem is the conditions of excavation in the city itself. The site of Rome has been so intensively built on for centuries that we find these traces of early occupation only in spots that happen not to have been disturbed. The foundations dug in the first and second centuries CE for the vast marble temples of the forum obliterated much of what then lay beneath the surface; the cellars of grand Renaissance houses cut through even more ancient remains in other parts of the city. So we have tiny snapshots, never the big picture. This is archaeology at its most difficult, and - although new fragments of evidence emerge all the time - its interpretation, and reinterpretation is almost always contested and often controversial. For example, there is an ongoing debate about whether the small pieces of wattle and daub found in excavations in the Forum in the mid-20th century indicate that there was an early hut settlement there too, or whether they were inadvertently introduced as part of the rubble used a few centuries later to provide a new raised surface for the area. It has to be said that this place, though fine for a cemetery, would have been rather damp and marshy for a village.

(E) Precise dating is even more contentious. It cannot be stressed enough that there is no certain independent date for any of the archaeological material from earliest Rome or the area around, and that arguments still rage about the age of almost every major find. It has taken decades of work over the past century or so - using such diagnostics as the existence of wheel-made pottery (assumed to be later than handmade), the occasional presence on graves of Greek ceramics (whose dating is better, but still not perfectly understood) and careful comparison from site to site - to produce a rough chronological scheme covering the period from around 1000 to 600 BCE.

(F) On that basis, the earliest burials in Rome would have been around 1000 BCE, and the earliest known settlements around 750-700 BCE. But even these dates are far from certain. Recent scientific methods - including radiocarbon dating, which calculates the age of any organic material - have suggested that they are all too 'young', by as much as a hundred years. The building at Fidenae, for example, was dated around the middle of the eighth century BCE according to traditional archaeological criteria, but that is pushed back to around the end of the ninth century BCE if we follow radiocarbon analysis. If anything, Rome appears to be getting older.
parts.questions:
Questions 27-32
Do the following statements agree with the views of the writer in Reading Passage 3?
In boxes 27–32 on your answer sheet, write:

Q27 Historians have expressed little curiosity about the rise of the Roman Empire.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q28 Accounts from the first century BCE of Rome's origins may be less reliable than 21st-century accounts.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q29 Most Roman historians viewed their ancient capital in an unrealistically positive light.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q30 The accounts by early Roman historians about the founding of Rome provide a full description of life at that time.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q31 It is certain that the city of Rome was in existence long before 63 BCE.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q32 Some people oppose archaeological excavations in Rome because they can damage the ancient monuments.

  • A YES
  • B ​​​NO
  • C NOT GIVEN
Questions 33–36
Choose the correct answer.

Q33 According to the writer, why were the archaeological remains found at Fidenae important?

  • A They shed some light on the way of life of ancient Romans.
  • B They were the first evidence of an ancient Roman settlement in the area.
  • C They overturned common assumptions about the diet of ancient Romans.
  • D They showed how sophisticated domestic Roman architecture could be.

Q34 What did Rome's marble temples and Renaissance houses have in common?

  • A They were the most enduring buildings of their respective eras.
  • B They were evidence of Rome's enormous wealth.
  • C They were built on previously unoccupied sites.
  • D Their construction destroyed evidence of earlier buildings.

Q35 What does the writer say in the fifth paragraph about the dating of excavated remains?

  • A Only the age of a proportion of remains can be agreed upon.
  • B Only an approximate sequence of eras can be established.
  • C Serious attempts at dating began only a few decades ago.
  • D More thorough investigations will result in reliable dates.

Q36 In the final paragraph, the writer makes the point that

  • A traditional archaeological methods of dating have been discredited.
  • B many archaeologists are reluctant to abandon traditional methods of dating.
  • C radiocarbon dating is more accurate than archaeological methods.
  • D the findings of traditional archaeology and radiocarbon dating differ.
Questions 37–40
Complete each sentence with the correct ending, A-F, below.
37 The Latin language can be
38 The Roman Forum was
39 The recently discovered building at Fidenae was
40 Ancient Greek pottery is sometimes
  • A composed of organic materials which are in use in the 21st century.
  • B referred to in popular legends about the origins of Rome.
  • C constructed on the site of an earlier burial ground.
  • D used to determine the relative dates of various Roman artefacts.
  • E chosen as the area for the greatest number of archaeological excavations.
  • F expected to shed some light on what Rome was originally like.

reference:
Q27

解析 原文说历史学家从古至今一直在探究罗马为何能发展并控制庞大帝国，这与题目说的“几乎没有好奇心（little curiosity）”完全相反。

干扰 你可能会在匆忙中漏掉“little”带有否定含义，误以为是“有一点好奇心”。

句子 From ancient times to the present, historians have asked the question: How and why did an ordinary little town in central Italy grow so much bigger than any other in the ancient Mediterranean and come to control such a huge empire?

Q28

解析 原文明确提到公元前一世纪的历史学家掌握的直接证据，在某些方面甚至比现代（21世纪）作家还要少。

句子 During the first century BCE, Roman writers themselves began systematically to study the earlier centuries of their city and their empire. Yet these historians had little more direct evidence of the earliest phases of Rome's history than modern writers have, and in some ways perhaps not as much, as there were no surviving documents or archives.

Q29

解析 原文提到罗马历史学家的著作反映了他们如何看待自己的城市、价值观和缺点，但并没有提及他们是否带有“不切实际的积极（unrealistically positive）”眼光。

句子 Their 'histories' about the foundation of ancient Rome tell us a good deal about how the Romans saw their city, their values, and their failings.

Q30

解析 原文直接指出这些历史学家的记录关于早期罗马实际生活面貌的内容“非常少（very little indeed）”，这直接打脸了题目中说的“全面描述（full description）”。

句子 Their 'histories' about the foundation of ancient Rome tell us a good deal about how the Romans saw their city, their values, and their failings. However, they tell us very little indeed about what they claim to inform us about: that is, what earliest Rome was actually like.

Q31

解析 原文明确且肯定地说，在公元前63年，罗马已经是一座“非常古老（very old）”的城市了，这证实了它在63 BCE之前很久就已经存在。

句子 One fact is obvious. Rome was already a very old city by 63 BCE, the birth date of its first emperor.

Q32

解析 原文只提到了在古迹下方进行挖掘能发现早期定居点的痕迹，但整篇文章都没有提到“有人反对（oppose）”挖掘工作会破坏古迹。

干扰 你可能会根据常识自己脑补“挖掘会破坏文物”，但做判断题绝不能脱离原文已有信息。

句子 Dig down deep in the city of Rome, below the visible ancient monuments, and a few traces of a much earlier settlement or settlements remain.

Q33

解析 原文说人们对早期的生活方式知之甚少，但是在Fidenae发现的建筑里有中央壁炉、陶罐以及食物和家畜的痕迹，这正好填补了空白（fill in some of the gaps），也就是选项A说的“揭示了古罗马人的生活方式”。

句子 We have little idea of the nature of these huts beyond their construction in wood, clay, and thatch, and still less of the lifestyle they supported. But we can fill in some of the gaps if we look just outside Rome. One of the best preserved and most carefully excavated of these early structures was found at Fidenae... Inside was a central hearth, some large pottery storage jars, and traces of predictable foodstuffs and domestic animals.

Q34

解析 原文提到大理石神庙的地基“抹去了（obliterated）”地下的遗迹，文艺复兴时期房屋的地窖也“切穿了（cut through）”更古老的遗骸，这就等同于它们都破坏了早期建筑的证据。

句子 The foundations dug in the first and second centuries CE for the vast marble temples of the forum obliterated much of what then lay beneath the surface; the cellars of grand Renaissance houses cut through even more ancient remains in other parts of the city. So we have tiny snapshots, never the big picture.

Q35

解析 原文强调精确测定年代很有争议，花了几十年时间也只是制定出了一个“粗略的年代顺序表（rough chronological scheme）”，对应选项的“只能建立一个大致的时代顺序”。

句子 Precise dating is even more contentious. It cannot be stressed enough that there is no certain independent date for any of the archaeological material from earliest Rome or the area around, and that arguments still rage about the age of almost every major find. It has taken decades of work over the past century or so... to produce a rough chronological scheme covering the period from around 1000 to 600 BCE.

Q36

解析 原文通过Fidenae建筑的例子，明确对比了“传统考古标准”和“放射性碳分析”得出的年代结果不同（相差约一百年），说明两者的发现存在差异（differ）。

句子 Recent scientific methods - including radiocarbon dating, which calculates the age of any organic material - have suggested that they are all too 'young', by as much as a hundred years. The building at Fidenae, for example, was dated around the middle of the eighth century BCE according to traditional archaeological criteria, but that is pushed back to around the end of the ninth century BCE if we follow radiocarbon analysis.

Q37

解析 原文指出要在拉丁语中寻找线索，以追溯早期罗马的特征（point back to features of earliest Rome），对应选项“有望揭示罗马最初的样貌”。

干扰 不要因为看到其他选项里的原词就乱选，紧盯原文中“Latin language”后面的动作指向，去寻找同义替换。

句子 One way of doing this is by turning away from the histories of Roman writers and seeking out clues in the Latin language, or in later Roman institutions that might point back to features of earliest Rome.

Q38

解析 原文说罗马广场（Forum）正下方躺着早期墓地（cemetery）的遗迹，这就说明它是建在早期的墓地（burial ground = cemetery）之上的。

句子 Beneath the Forum itself (an ancient marketplace at the centre of the city) lie the remains of an early cemetery, which caused tremendous excitement when they were first unearthed at the start of the 20th century.

Q39

解析 原文提到Fidenae的建筑是由木头（一种有机材料）建造的，并且这种建造方法直到今天（up to the present day，也就是21世纪）仍在使用。

句子 One of the best preserved and most carefully excavated of these early structures was found at Fidenae... It is a rectangular building, some six by five metres, made of wood and rammed earth - a construction method still utilised up to the present day - with a simple porch around it, formed by the overhanging roof.

Q40

解析 原文说利用希腊陶器（Greek ceramics/pottery）在墓穴中的出现以及遗址间的比较，来制定一个粗略的年代顺序（chronological scheme），也就是选项说的“用来测定相对年代”。

干扰 你可能会觉得这段话很长抓不住重点，其实只要定位到“Greek ceramics”，直接跳过括号里的废话，往后看破折号连接的总结性短语“produce a rough chronological scheme”就能锁定答案。

句子 It has taken decades of work over the past century or so - using such diagnostics as the existence of wheel-made pottery (assumed to be later than handmade), the occasional presence on graves of Greek ceramics (whose dating is better, but still not perfectly understood) and careful comparison from site to site - to produce a rough chronological scheme covering the period from around 1000 to 600 BCE.
